answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes moved from four to three releases per year (officially changed in April 2021, with 1.22 the first longer-cycle release) for several stated reasons:

- **Growing burden from each release.** As the project matured, the number of enhancements per cycle grew. That added work for contributors and the Release Engineering team.
- **Pressure on downstream users.** Consumers and integrators struggled to keep up with ever more feature-packed releases. Wider adoption meant a bigger downstream chain was affected.
- **Longer support per release.** Users and integrators get longer support terms for each minor version, because the previous three releases are supported for a longer period. One release lead noted that the last three releases can now be supported across a full calendar year instead of 9 of 12 months.
- **More time to mature features.** Contributors get more time to mature enhancements and get them production-ready.
- **Less management overhead for SIG Release.** This frees the team to improve release quality and tooling. The KEP adds that only 3 patch releases need maintaining instead of up to 4 overlapping. It also allows smoother release-team transitions and possibly more shadows.

The move was also described as balancing how contributions and releases are managed against the community's ability to plan upgrades and stay current.

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer: The built-in Pod Security admission controller (Pod Security Admission, the PodSecurity admission plugin) enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree. It applies restrictions at the namespace level when pods are created, with policy enforcement controlled through namespace labels. The three policies are privileged, baseline and restricted. Policies can be applied in enforce, audit and warn modes. Cluster-wide defaults and exemptions (by username, RuntimeClass or namespace) can be set through an AdmissionConfiguration passed to kube-apiserver via --admission-control-config-file. The controller is enabled by default and has been stable since v1.25, after alpha in v1.22 and beta in v1.23. It replaces the removed PodSecurityPolicy and can be combined with admission webhooks.

answer.question: Why was PodSecurityPolicy replaced instead of fixed?
answer.answer: PodSecurityPolicy was replaced rather than fixed because the updates needed to improve its usability would have introduced breaking changes, so it was removed (in v1.25, after being deprecated in v1.21) in favor of a more user-friendly replacement: Pod Security Admission, which went stable in v1.25 (chunk 39918). The replacement was designed around a different approach. There is already a strong ecosystem of external admission controllers, so PSP's successor did not need to be all things to all people. A built-in controller's key advantage is simplicity of deployment and adoption. The new design aims to be as simple as practical while still flexible enough for production use. It offers soft rollout features for retrofitting existing clusters and can be partially or fully deactivated to coexist with external admission controllers (chunks 37029, 37013). Pod Security Admission is an in-tree plugin that enforces the pod security standards at the namespace level. It makes basic pod security easier to enforce without deep security knowledge, and it can be combined with third-party solutions for more sophisticated cases (chunk 39961). All of this comes from blog posts (tier 6); the evidence includes no docs or KEP text on the rationale.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer: Yes, but only before version 1.24. Before 1.24, Kubernetes automatically generated Secret-based tokens for ServiceAccounts. Such an auto-generated legacy token is recognised by being referenced in the ServiceAccount's `secrets` field. In 1.24 the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate became beta and enabled by default. With it enabled, Secret API objects containing service account tokens are no longer auto-generated for every ServiceAccount. Instead, use the TokenRequest API to get tokens. If you need a non-expiring token, create a Secret yourself for the token controller to populate. KEP-2799 describes this as changing the Token Controller so it does not auto-create these secrets. Beginning in 1.29, legacy tokens that were auto-generated are marked invalid if they stay unused for a set period (one year by default). If they remain unused for a further such period, the control plane purges them.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer:
KEP-2799 explains that once BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume went GA in 1.22, Pods got their service account tokens through the TokenRequest API and stored them in a projected volume. That made auto-generating Secret-based tokens unnecessary, and the KEP says those tokens are less secure than bound tokens. The docs add that TokenRequest tokens have bounded lifetimes and are invalidated automatically when their Pod is deleted. The 1.29 release blog likewise calls the time-limited, pod-bound tokens more secure.

As a result, the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature stopped the token controller from auto-creating these Secrets. It was beta and on by default in 1.24. You can still create a long-lived token Secret by hand if you need one, but TokenRequest is recommended instead.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer:
Yes, as of the current releases (1.36 onward, including 1.37). The StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate was alpha and off by default in 1.33–1.35. It became beta and on by default in 1.36. With it enabled, the kube-apiserver rejects IPv4 addresses whose octets have leading zeros (e.g. `010.000.000.005`), and CIDR values containing such IPs, in API fields. It also rejects IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses and ambiguous CIDR values such as `192.168.0.5/24`.

The stricter validation covers only fields in built-in API kinds. It does not cover custom resource kinds, values in Kubernetes configuration files, or command-line arguments.

If the gate is disabled, such values are still accepted, but the API server returns a warning that they will be rejected in the future.

This replaces older behaviour: the 1.23 changelog said Kubernetes would keep allowing leading zeros for compatibility.

The KEP claims the feature is stable, but at 1.37 the observed stage is beta (on by default). This was resolved in favour of the observed stage.

answer.question: Before strict IP validation was on by default, what happened when a Service used an IPv4 address with leading zeros?
answer.answer:
Before `StrictIPCIDRValidation` became default-on, Service IPv4 addresses with leading zeros were accepted. The gate was alpha and off by default from 1.33 to 1.35, then went to beta and on by default in 1.36.

- **How they were parsed:** Kubernetes deliberately kept allowing leading zeros for compatibility, even though Go 1.17's `net.ParseIP`/`net.ParseCIDR` rejected them. Kubernetes read the octets as decimal, dropping the extra zeros, so "012.000.001.002" became 12.0.1.2. Most libc-based code would instead read those octets as octal (10.0.1.2). That mismatch is the issue behind CVE-2021-29923.
- **Warnings:** Service IP/CIDR fields have returned API server warnings since 1.27, for example: non-standard IP address "05.06.07.08" will be considered invalid in a future Kubernetes release: use "5.6.7.8". Likewise, while the gate was disabled, creating an object with such a value produced a warning that it will be rejected in the future, but the object was still created.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
According to the KEP, validation of IP and CIDR strings in API fields had been too lax. It accepted any string that Go's `net.ParseIP` and `net.ParseCIDR` would accept, even when some of those strings had ambiguous meanings that could cause security problems.

Go 1.17 changed how it handles IPv4 addresses with leading "0"s, to avoid CVE-2021-29923. After that, there was consensus that Kubernetes should eventually make API validation stricter too. It was not done right away because the project did not want to retroactively invalidate existing API objects. KEP-4858 is the plan for finally doing it.

The feature-gate docs give the concrete concern. Values such as IPv4 octets with leading zeros, or IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses like `::ffff:192.168.0.1`, can be interpreted by different components as different IP addresses. That is why `StrictIPCIDRValidation` forbids them.

The KEP's goal is to avoid security problems from ambiguously parsable IPs and CIDRs. It says the stricter validation should make such values impossible in the future, at least in new clusters.

The v1.36 release blog post (lowest authority) adds a secondary benefit: catching malformed addresses that could cause confusing runtime behavior or configuration bugs.

heading_path: Why we decided to change the release cadence
What this means for end users

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
According to KEP-1498, the extension from 9 months to roughly a year (formally 14 months: about 12 months of support plus a 2-month upgrade period) was driven by end-user needs.

- **Annual business cycles.** Financial, certification, sales, vacation and HR cycles are overwhelmingly annual. Many users therefore want at least annual support cycles from the projects they depend on. Nine months is an irregular period compared with most companies' planning, operations and financial cycles.
- **Users falling out of support.** A WG LTS survey in early 2019 found that a significant subset of users (about a third) did not upgrade within the 9-month window. They had production machines on unsupported versions.
- **Expected coverage gain.** The survey suggested that a 12–14 month window would let those users stay supported. This would raise the share of users on supported versions from 50–60% to more than 80%.
- **Constant upgrade planning.** With a new minor release every three months, users face a constant need to evaluate, plan and move forward under the deprecation and version skew policies.
- **A small, viable first step.** The KEP saw extending toward a year as a relatively minor change that was viable to implement. It called it a meaningful first response to users. Keeping the change small would also let the project discover the unknowns of changing support windows.
- **Formalizing existing practice.** The 14 months also formalized the existing practice of keeping patch branch CI running 6–7 weeks beyond the 9 months, as a failsafe for critical CVEs or upgrade blockers.

The KEP planned 1.19 as the first release to get a year of patch support.

answer.question: How do I configure the kube-apiserver to use more than one authorization webhook?
answer.answer:
Use a structured authorization configuration file rather than the command-line flags. Multiple webhooks, webhook failure policy and CEL pre-filter rules are only available through that file. With `--authorization-mode`, you can only enable one webhook in the chain.

Steps:
1. Write an `AuthorizationConfiguration` file (apiVersion `apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1`) with an `authorizers` list.
   - You may add several entries of `type: Webhook`, but at most one authorizer of each other type (for example `Node` and `RBAC`).
   - The chain is evaluated in the order the authorizers appear in the file.
2. Give each webhook entry a `name` (required, used in metrics) and a `webhook` block with:
   - `timeout` (required, max 30s);
   - `subjectAccessReviewVersion` (required; v1beta1 or v1);
   - `matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion` (v1);
   - `failurePolicy` (required; `NoOpinion` continues to later authorizers, `Deny` rejects the request);
   - `connectionInfo`, for example `type: KubeConfigFile` with `kubeConfigFile: /path/to/webhook-kubeconfig.yaml`. The webhook kubeconfig file names the remote service under "clusters" and the API server's credentials under "users". `InClusterConfig` is not allowed for kube-apiserver.
   - Optional: `authorizedTTL` / `unauthorizedTTL` and `cacheAuthorizedRequests` / `cacheUnauthorizedRequests` for caching.
   - Optional: `matchConditions`, which are CEL expressions on the `request` (SubjectAccessReview) that decide whether the webhook is called at all (up to 64).
3. Start kube-apiserver with `--authorization-config=<path>`. Do not also pass `--authorization-mode`, because the two flags cannot be combined.

The API server automatically reloads the authorizer chain when the file changes.

Abridged example: `authorizers: [{type: Webhook, name: webhook, webhook: {...failurePolicy: Deny, connectionInfo: {type: KubeConfigFile, kubeConfigFile: /kube-system-authz-webhook.yaml}}}, {type: Node, name: node}, {type: RBAC, name: rbac}, {type: Webhook, name: in-cluster-authorizer, ...}]`.

This is the StructuredAuthorizationConfiguration feature (KEP-3221, which claims stable as of v1.32).

answer.question: Can I write an RBAC rule that explicitly denies a permission?
answer.answer: No. RBAC permissions are purely additive: a Role or ClusterRole holds rules that grant permissions, and there are no "deny" rules. The Authorization docs say the same thing: Kubernetes RBAC does not provide negative (deny) access rules. One consequence is that `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow,RBAC` has the same effect as `AlwaysAllow` alone. If RBAC does not allow a request, the API server goes on to the next configured authorizer. For example, with RBAC and ABAC run in parallel, a request allowed by either policy is allowed. To limit access, grant only the specific resources and verbs that are needed (least privilege) rather than trying to subtract permissions.

heading_path: Migration from command line arguments to configuration file

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes add a structured authentication configuration file instead of keeping the --oidc-* flags?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes did not simply replace the --oidc-* flags. The flags still work and are still supported, but you cannot combine them with --authentication-config: if both are set, the API server reports an error and exits. SIG Auth recommends migrating to the configuration file.

The file was added because the flag-based OIDC authenticator could not provide customizations users wanted. KEP-3331's goals list them:
- Claim validation rules beyond the audience claim, which the flags could only match by exact value.
- Richer claim mappings, including nested claims. The flags could only pick a single value from a single claim and prefix groups.
- More than one OIDC provider and more than one client ID, without an external provider that handles multiplexing (such as Dex).
- Changing authenticator settings without restarting kube-apiserver.
- Validation rules on the final user info object, so infra providers can safely expose this to customers.
- Easy migration from the existing OIDC flags.

The blog posts add that a file gives more flexibility than command-line options and makes further improvements easier to deliver. answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer:
As of 1.37, kube-proxy's ipvs mode still works, but it has been deprecated since v1.35. It is only available on Linux nodes. The plan is: from v1.40 it is disabled by default, and you can turn it back on with the KubeProxyIPVS feature gate. Without that override, kube-proxy in ipvs mode exits with an error. In v1.43 the ipvs mode is removed completely. Starting kube-proxy in ipvs mode already prints a deprecation warning, and kubeadm adds its own warning in 1.37.

What to use instead: the nftables mode, which became GA in 1.33. It is the recommended replacement and performs better than both iptables and ipvs. If your Linux kernel is too old for nftables, use iptables mode rather than ipvs. iptables is still the default, and its performance has improved a lot. The KEP notes that all kernels too old for nftables mode will be out of LTS by the end of 2026.

answer.question: Should a new controller watch Endpoints or EndpointSlices to find a Service's backends?
answer.answer:
Watch EndpointSlices. As of v1.33 the Endpoints API is deprecated, and the docs recommend that all clients use the EndpointSlice API instead. The docs give three problems with Endpoints: it does not support dual-stack clusters, it lacks information needed for newer features such as trafficDistribution, and it truncates the endpoint list when it is too long for one object. Since 1.22 that limit is 1000 endpoints, and the object is labelled `endpoints.kubernetes.io/over-capacity: truncated` when truncation happens. The API server also returns deprecation warnings when Endpoints are read or written.

Kube-proxy and Gateway API implementations already use EndpointSlices only. KEP-4974, an unshipped proposal, aims for clusters to run with the Endpoints and EndpointSlice mirroring controllers disabled. In that setup, Endpoints objects would no longer be produced for Services.

When consuming EndpointSlices, note that a Service can have any number of slices. Select them with the `kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>` label. Expect several slices when the Service is dual-stack (one per IP family), when endpoints target different ports (for example during a rollout), or when there are more than 100 endpoints.

One side note on mirroring: the docs and KEP-752's test plan disagree on how the skip-mirror label works. The tier-1 docs win: Endpoints are mirrored unless `endpointslice.kubernetes.io/skip-mirror` is set to `true`. Either way, user-written Endpoints for selectorless Services generally reach consumers as mirrored EndpointSlices, though the docs say up to 1000 addresses per subset are mirrored.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20 dual-stack was not on by default (it was alpha, reimplemented in 1.20 to support dual-stack Services), so you had to enable the IPv6DualStack feature gate on the relevant components and set dual-stack cluster network assignments:
- kube-apiserver: --feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true" and --service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>
- kube-controller-manager: --feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true", --cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>, --service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR> (--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4/--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6 default to /24 and /64)
- kubelet: --feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"
- kube-proxy: --cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR> and --feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"
Prerequisites: Kubernetes 1.20 or later, provider support for routable IPv4/IPv6 node interfaces, and a network plugin that supports dual-stack (such as Kubenet or Calico). Once enabled, you could create Services using IPv4, IPv6 or both, and change that setting on existing Services. Only from 1.21 (beta) did the gate default to enabled.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how could a Service prefer endpoints on the same node as the client?
answer.answer:
In Kubernetes 1.20, Service Topology (an alpha feature since v1.17) lets you do this. With Service Topology enabled, you set the `topologyKeys` field on the Service spec. It is a preference-ordered list of Node labels used to sort endpoints. Traffic goes to a Node whose value for the first label matches the originating Node's value for that label. If no backend matches, the next label is tried, and so on.

To prefer node-local endpoints, list `"kubernetes.io/hostname"` first:
- `["kubernetes.io/hostname"]` sends traffic only to endpoints on the same node. If none exists there, the connection fails, because when no key matches, traffic is rejected as if the Service had no backends.
- `["kubernetes.io/hostname", "*"]` prefers node-local endpoints but falls back to any endpoint in the cluster. The special value `"*"` means "any topology" and only makes sense as the last entry.
- You can also add intermediate fallbacks, e.g. `["kubernetes.io/hostname", "topology.kubernetes.io/zone", "topology.kubernetes.io/region", "*"]`.

Example:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
  topologyKeys:
    - "kubernetes.io/hostname"
    - "*"
```

If `topologyKeys` is unset or empty, no topology constraints apply.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer:
kube-proxy's nftables mode became generally available (GA) in Kubernetes v1.33. Even after GA, iptables stayed the default mode. You select nftables by passing `--proxy-mode nftables` or by setting `mode: nftables` in the config file. The CHANGELOG for 1.37 again states that nftables became GA in v1.33, and the KEP-3866 chunks show it as stable.

The path to GA:
- **Alpha, v1.29.** A new nftables-based backend was added. The iptables-based default had unsolvable problems, iptables development had mostly stopped, and some Linux distributions had started deprecating and removing iptables.
- **Beta, v1.31.** The mode sat behind the `NFTablesProxyMode` feature gate, which was now enabled by default. It is only available on Linux nodes and requires kernel 5.13 or later.

KEP-3866's graduation criteria set the bar for each step. Beta required at least two releases since alpha, no major outstanding bugs, mode-switching and perf e2e jobs, and documentation of behavior differences. GA required at least two releases since beta, non-trivial real-world usage, no bugs that would make them hesitate to recommend it, and a plan for next steps.

What followed GA:
- In v1.35, ipvs mode was deprecated, with nftables recommended as its replacement.
- In v1.37, kubeadm explicitly sets the mode to iptables when no mode is given, and kube-proxy warns when the mode isn't set explicitly. This is part of a planned move to nftables as the default in a future release.

answer.question: How did support for multiple Service CIDRs (ServiceCIDR objects) progress through its release stages?
answer.answer:
Multiple Service CIDR support (ServiceCIDR/IPAddress objects) is controlled by the MultiCIDRServiceAllocator feature gate. Its progression was:

- **Alpha, v1.27–v1.30:** disabled by default.
- **Beta, v1.31–v1.32:** still disabled by default. Users had to enable the feature gate and the networking v1beta1 API group to dynamically reconfigure Service CIDR ranges. Also in 1.31, the new allocators began using a dual-write strategy by default, which avoids duplicate IPs across skewed kube-apiservers. Users could opt out by enabling the DisableAllocatorDualWrite gate.
- **Stable (GA), v1.33 onward:** enabled by default and locked. In the same release DisableAllocatorDualWrite moved to beta (disabled by default). The 1.33 release notes flagged action required for administrators and distributions: with ServiceCIDR objects, they may want to restrict overlapping or extra ranges, for example with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

There is one disagreement in the sources. An early, unshipped KEP draft targeted alpha for 1.25 and still claims alpha. The observed gate history (alpha from 1.27, stable from 1.33) takes precedence over that claim.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer:
According to KEP-3866 and related sources, the reasons were:

- **iptables is stagnating.** The default Linux kube-proxy was based on iptables. Problems with iptables led to its successor, nftables. Development on iptables has mostly stopped, and new features and performance improvements go mainly into nftables. [29878, 43088]
- **Distros are dropping iptables.** Some Linux distributions had already started to deprecate and remove iptables. nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems. [43088] The KEP warns that doing nothing would eventually leave many users unable to use the default proxy implementation. [29958]
- **Two backends could become one.** SIG Network was supporting both the iptables and ipvs backends. It felt it couldn't drop ipvs because of perceived performance issues with iptables. A backend as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as fast as ipvs could eventually let both be deprecated, leaving only one Linux backend to support. [29885]
- **It would drive code cleanup.** There was a desire for a "kube-proxy library" that third parties could build on (KEP-3786). The existing core kube-proxy code was not designed well enough to support that. Writing a new backend would force a review of the shared code and might suggest ways to clean it up, rationalize it and optimize it. [29886]
- **Existing implementations weren't suitable.** None of the three existing nftables-based kube-proxy implementations could be adopted directly or used as a starting point:
  - kube-nftlb adds an extra nftlb layer and was unmaintained since November 2020.
  - nfproxy is not feature-complete and was unmaintained since January 2021.
  - kpng's nft backend is a proof of concept that doesn't use nftables features well and relies on kpng APIs without upstream consensus. [29891]

A later blog post adds performance detail. iptables updates remain O(n) in the total number of Services, even after the optimizations that began in 1.26. nftables updates are only O(n) in what changed since the last sync. Each component gets its own private table, so there is no global lock contention. [44770]
